analysis.disclaimer: The event analysis is assisted by an AI model and can be wrong, in both directions (an attack taken for normal use, or the reverse). Its conclusions are suggestions only: loosening (exclusions, allowing) always needs a person's approval; only tightening (a new confident block) may apply on its own, and only when every check passed. Look at the evidence yourself before you approve.

analysis.intro: The self-hosted language model reviews recent WAF events on a schedule: paths to block outright, normal use that is wrongly blocked (an exclusion is proposed), and alerts someone has to follow up. compliance.ctl.account_management.desc: Accounts can have an end date and are disabled after it; accounts without a sign-in for the configured number of days are disabled automatically (never the last active administrator); the account review lists every account and token for the periodic review.
compliance.ctl.account_management.title: Account management
compliance.ctl.audit_logging.desc: Every action is recorded with time, actor, actor type, source address, action, result and details, and sent as one JSON line to syslog.
compliance.ctl.audit_logging.title: Audit logging
compliance.ctl.auth_feedback.desc: Passwords and codes are masked while typed; an unknown user and a wrong password get the same answer and the same response time.
compliance.ctl.auth_feedback.title: Authenticator feedback
compliance.ctl.authentication.desc: Passwords are stored as scrypt hashes; minimum length, character classes, history and minimum / maximum age are enforced; accounts are locked after repeated failures; a temporary password must be changed at the first sign-in.
compliance.ctl.authentication.title: Password authentication
compliance.ctl.backup.desc: A daily database backup is made with an integrity check and a SHA-256 file and kept for the configured days; copying the backups off the host is an organisational measure.
compliance.ctl.backup.title: Backup
compliance.ctl.change_management.desc: Rule changes go through static checks, evidence, a sandbox and an approval; a root program applies them with nginx -t, reload, health check and automatic restore; every version can be rolled back.
compliance.ctl.change_management.title: Change management
Every nginx, ModSecurity and CRS file, the nginx binary and the ModSecurity module are fingerprinted; every change is recorded and attributed, and manual edits of the managed rule files are detected.
compliance.ctl.data_at_rest.desc: The database is readable only by the service user (file 0600, directory 0700) and holds masked values only; it is not encrypted by the program, so use disk encryption where it is required.
compliance.ctl.data_at_rest.title: Stored data
compliance.ctl.data_masking.desc: Values of sensitive parameters (passwords, tokens, one-time codes…) are masked before anything is stored; there is no way to see the original.
compliance.ctl.data_masking.title: Masking of sensitive data
compliance.ctl.evidence_export.desc: The audit log can be exported with every hash and a summary hash and verified offline; event exports carry a SHA-256.
compliance.ctl.evidence_export.title: Evidence export
compliance.ctl.least_privilege.desc: Four roles (viewer, operator, approver, administrator). API tokens are limited to scopes and source networks and can never approve changes, manage tokens or change settings.
compliance.ctl.least_privilege.title: Least privilege
compliance.ctl.log_capacity.desc: Free disk space is checked against a minimum; events, statistics and the audit log have configured retention periods.
compliance.ctl.log_capacity.title: Log storage capacity
compliance.ctl.log_failure_response.desc: Integrity failures, failed backups and account lockouts are written as critical events (syslog priority 2) so the SIEM can alert; syslog delivery errors are counted on the system check.
compliance.ctl.log_protection.desc: Records are hash-chained and the table refuses changes and deletions; every few minutes the newest hash is anchored in an append-only file and in syslog, so a rewritten chain is detected.
compliance.ctl.log_protection.title: Protection of the audit log
compliance.ctl.monitoring.desc: The web application firewall events themselves: blocked and logged requests by site, attack type, source and rule, plus every configuration change.
compliance.ctl.monitoring.title: Monitoring
compliance.ctl.multi_factor.desc: Time-based one-time codes (TOTP) are required for the configured roles (by default approver and administrator), with protection against reusing a code.
compliance.ctl.multi_factor.title: Two-factor authentication
compliance.ctl.retention.desc: Events and statistics are deleted after the configured days; the audit log is kept forever by default, and a configured purge keeps the remaining chain verifiable.
compliance.ctl.retention.title: Retention
compliance.ctl.secure_development.desc: The backend uses the Python standard library only; the interface has a strict content security policy and shows request data as text only; automated tests and a release check (privacy scan, tests) run before every release.
compliance.ctl.secure_development.title: Secure development
compliance.ctl.segregation_of_duties.des: Whoever proposes a change cannot approve it. Single-admin mode (recorded in the audit log) allows it, with a fresh one-time code and a written reason for any loosening.
compliance.ctl.session_timeout.desc: Idle sessions are signed out automatically, every session has a maximum lifetime, and the number of sessions per user is limited.
compliance.ctl.session_timeout.title: Session timeout
compliance.ctl.siem_forwarding.desc: Audit records and anchors are written to the local syslog as JSON; forwarding them to the SIEM and the alert rules are set up in the syslog daemon and the SIEM.
compliance.ctl.siem_forwarding.title: Forwarding to the SIEM
compliance.ctl.software_integrity.desc: Each release ships a manifest with the SHA-256 of every file, signed with the release key (RSA-3072). The installer verifies it and pins the key; the service and the root apply program check the installed files again, and the apply program refuses to run modified code.
compliance.ctl.software_integrity.title: Software integrity
compliance.ctl.time_sync.desc: Checks that the system clock is synchronised with a time source (NTP); audit times come from this clock.
compliance.ctl.time_sync.title: Time synchronisation
compliance.ctl.transport.desc: The service listens on loopback only and is reached through nginx over HTTPS; session cookies are Secure, HttpOnly and host-bound.
compliance.ctl.transport.title: Protection in transit
The versions of nginx and the CRS are shown; keeping the operating system, nginx, libmodsecurity and the CRS patched is an organisational measure.

error.own_change: You proposed this change: someone else has to approve it (or turn on single-admin mode).

error.password_same: The new password must differ from the current one.
error.password_too_recent: The password was changed recently; it can be changed again in about {hours} hours.

error.password_too_simple: The password needs at least {min_classes} kinds of characters (lower case, upper case, digits, other).
error.raw_admin_only: Expert rules are for administrators only.
error.rule_id_in_use: Rule id {rule_id} is already used (ids are never reused).
error.scanner_outside_internal: A known scanner must be inside the internal networks and no wider than /16 (IPv6 /48): {item}
error.scope_required: Choose the sites, or every site.
error.test_per_block: Every confident block needs its own external test expecting 403 whose path it matches.
error.token_source_not_allowed: This token may not be used from this address.
error.too_many_attempts: Too many attempts. Try again in {retry_after} seconds. This has been recorded.
error.too_many_rules: The file has more than {limit} rules; split it.
error.totp_invalid: The one-time code is wrong or expired.
error.totp_required_for_role: Your role requires two-factor authentication; it cannot be turned off.
error.user_exists: A user with this name already exists.
event.create_hint: Opens a draft; nothing changes until it passes the checks and is approved.
event.redacted_note: Sensitive fields (passwords, tokens…) are masked before they are stored. The original text is not kept.
event.truncated: This record was too large and was cut; some matches may be missing.
events.title: Events
evidence.attack_like_warning: This exclusion would also silence external requests that look like attacks. Make it narrower if you can.
evidence.block_rule: Passes when no external request it matches got a 2xx/3xx and no internal source other than known scanners matches.
evidence.country_note: Counted from the access logs with today's country lists (internal networks, known scanners, trusted proxies and the protected list excluded). Answered requests are real users the rule would shut out: check them before approving. The first row covers every log kept; when a limit already exists in nginx, the last days show what changes.
evidence.country_success_samples: Answered requests that would be refused
evidence.external_success_samples: External requests that succeeded (would now be blocked)
evidence.incomplete: The scan stopped at its time limit: the evidence is incomplete.
geoip.how_note: The web service never downloads anything: the update runs in its own restricted program, which checks MaxMind's SHA-256 and test-reads the file before using it. Internal addresses are never looked up.
geoip.last_run: Last update run: {at}. Files older than {days} days are downloaded again (daily check).
geoip.not_configured: Not set up yet: add a [geoip] section to {file} (create it if the file has none) with account_id = "<MaxMind account number>", put the license key alone in {key} (owner root, group jtwaf, mode 0640), then restart the service. A free GeoLite2 account is enough.
geoip.not_configured_ui: Not set up yet: enter the MaxMind account ID and license key in "GeoIP account" above and save.
geoip.title: GeoIP databases
guide.adopt.approve_d: Adoption is a change of its own and only an administrator can approve it.
guide.adopt.detect_d: The local Include files of the main ModSecurity file: the last one before the CRS rules and the first one after them.
guide.adopt.drift_fix: To fix it: if the edit was not wanted, either undo it on the server, or (approver) restore the files of the current version below — that overwrites the edit and is recorded in the audit trail. If the edit was wanted, restore first and then propose the same rule here as a change.
guide.adopt.drift_what: After every apply the hashes of the managed files are recorded. When a file on disk no longer matches the last applied version, someone edited it outside this system. Every change and restore is then refused (and recorded at priority crit), so the edit is never overwritten silently; the root apply program checks the same hashes again right before it writes.
guide.adopt.equiv_d: The sandbox sends recent distinct requests from the event history plus the regression samples through the current and the new configuration: every status code and matched rule must be identical.
guide.adopt.import_d: Every rule and comment block is copied unchanged, in file order.
guide.adopt.managed_d: From then on only this tool writes these files, and every change goes through checks and approval.
guide.adopt.switch_d: The apply program writes the two managed files, points the Include lines of the main ModSecurity file at them, then runs nginx -t, reload and the health checks.
guide.adopt.title: Adoption: from hand-made files to managed files
guide.analysis.approve_d: An approver approves or rejects it in Changes. A rejected path is not proposed again for 30 days.
guide.analysis.candidates_d: Events grouped by the path a rule sees (decoded, lowercase, no query). Kept with enough events and sources; left out when an existing rule or an open change covers the path, or a proposal for it was turned down in the last 30 days.
guide.analysis.checks_d: The usual checks: the rule itself, evidence from the access logs (no external 2xx/3xx, no internal requests) and the sandbox.
guide.analysis.events_d: WAF events of the last hours: external requests no confident rule stopped yet (attack probes), and requests the anomaly score blocked (false positives).
guide.analysis.llm_d: Sent to the configured LLM server in batches (at most 15 each), the answer constrained by a JSON schema: a verdict per path (attack probe, legitimate, unsure; for blocked requests false positive, attack, unsure), a confidence and a reason, plus a regular expression for attack probes. The request data is always marked untrusted.
guide.analysis.note: The analysis never approves and never writes rules itself. Loosening (exclusions for false positives) and blocks that include internal sources always wait for a person; only external confident blocks apply by themselves, when you turn on "Apply the event analysis' confident blocks automatically too" and the evidence and sandbox checks pass.
guide.analysis.propose_d: Only a few per run: external confident blocks and the narrowest exclusions, proposed as ordinary changes by "analyst"; what needs following up becomes an alert and is notified.
guide.analysis.title: How the analysis works
guide.analysis.validate_d: The program decides, not the model: only attack probes with enough confidence; the regex must start with ^, match the path, and not match common paths, paths judged legitimate or regression samples.
guide.apply.drift_d: The managed files must still be the ones the change was prepared against; otherwise it refuses.
guide.apply.health_after_d: The same URLs again: every status code must be unchanged.
guide.apply.health_before_d: Requests every health check URL through this nginx and notes the status codes.
guide.apply.note: Any failure from the write on puts the snapshot back, runs nginx -t and reloads again: the change shows “apply failed (restored)”. A failure before the snapshot (bad request, manual edit) changes nothing.
guide.apply.reload_d: Reloads nginx, confirms that new worker processes started, then waits for the old ones to finish.
guide.apply.request_d: Checksums, allowed directives and the rule ID range are checked again; nginx must be running its installed binary.
guide.apply.snapshot_d: Copies the current files aside so they can be put back.
guide.apply.title: Inside the apply program
guide.apply.write_d: Writes the new managed files (adoption: also points the main ModSecurity file at them).
guide.arch.hint: Click a box (or focus it and press Enter) to read what it does.
guide.arch.service: service user jtwaf, listens on 127.0.0.1 only
guide.arch.title: Architecture
guide.audit.alert_d: A failure writes integrity.audit_chain_failed at syslog priority crit, repeated every 12 hours while it lasts, and a _recovered record once it is fixed.
guide.audit.anchor_d: Every few minutes (default 5, [integrity] anchor_minutes) the newest record number and hash are appended to the anchor file (append-only, chattr +a) and sent to syslog for the SIEM. Each record also goes to syslog with its hash.
guide.audit.chain_d: Each record stores sha256(previous record's hash + this record). Changing, inserting or removing a record breaks the chain from that point on.
guide.audit.note: Export gives every record with its hashes, so the file can be checked offline with the audit-verify command shown after the export.
guide.audit.row_d: Sign-ins, changes, approvals, settings and system tasks each write one record (time, who, from where, what, result). The table only accepts new records: database triggers refuse changes and deletions.
guide.audit.title: How the audit trail is protected
guide.audit.verify_d: New records are checked at every anchor run, the whole chain once a day, and on demand with "Verify chain" or "Run checks now".
guide.cfgchg.cause_d: Applied version: only managed files changed, they match the last applied version and a version was applied around that time. Anything else: outside.
guide.cfgchg.compare_d: If the overall fingerprint differs from the last snapshot, the added, removed and changed files are listed. The first snapshot is the baseline.
guide.cfgchg.note: Look at every outside change: who made it and why.
guide.cfgchg.record_d: A new snapshot is saved and a config.changed audit record is written (result "outside" for outside changes).
guide.cfgchg.scan_d: Every few minutes (default 5, [integrity] config_check_minutes) the SHA-256 of every nginx, ModSecurity, CRS and managed file and of the nginx program is taken.
guide.cfgchg.title: How configuration changes are found
guide.cfgchg.warn_d: An outside change makes System check show a warning for 7 days.
guide.change.apply_d: The root apply program saves the current files, writes the new ones, runs nginx -t and reloads.
guide.change.approve_d: Loosening always needs a person, by default not the proposer. Tightening is applied automatically only if an admin turned that on, under strict conditions.
guide.change.checks_d: Static checks (regex sanity, too broad, ReDoS shape, rule-id ranges) and what the change would have done to past traffic.
guide.change.note: Every step is in the audit trail, and every apply keeps a version you can roll back to.
guide.change.propose_d: Pick a template (exclusion, confident block, redaction, plugin toggle, expert rule) and the narrowest scope.
guide.change.sandbox_d: A temporary nginx on 127.0.0.1 runs the test requests and the regression samples.
guide.change.title: From proposal to production
guide.change.verify_d: It confirms the reload took effect and the health-check URLs answer as before; any failure restores the previous files.
guide.compliance.fix_d: Edit {path}, restart the service, then Refresh. "Download JSON" keeps the result as evidence.
guide.compliance.level_d_set: Set to {level} by [compliance] level in config.toml. Higher levels add stricter requirements.
guide.compliance.level_d_unset: Not set ([compliance] level in config.toml): controls are judged on the basic checks only. medium and high add stricter requirements, such as password rules, dormant accounts and, at high, two-factor authentication for every role.
guide.compliance.live_d: Each control is computed now from the running configuration and the latest integrity checks, not from a questionnaire.
guide.compliance.needs_d: Under a gap or a partial control, the list names the setting or step that would close it, for example auth.password_history>=3.
guide.compliance.note: Each control cites ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A, the Taiwan protection baseline and OWASP Top 10:2025. Only what the code actually does is claimed.
guide.compliance.status_d: Met: done by the software. Partial: done in part. Gap: missing at this level. Organisational measure: needs a process outside the software (for example SIEM review or patching).
guide.compliance.title: How to read this page
guide.crs.compare_d: The total is compared with the inbound threshold ({n}).
guide.crs.pl_d: Rules up to this level count toward blocking; rules up to a higher detection level only add to the log. Higher levels catch more, and cause more false positives.
guide.crs.points_d: By severity: critical 5, error 4, warning 3, notice 2 (CRS defaults).
guide.crs.result_d: At or over the threshold: 403 if the engine is on for that request; in detection-only mode it is only logged.
guide.crs.title: How OWASP CRS scores a request
guide.cstate.apply_failed: Applying failed; the previous files were restored automatically.
guide.cstate.applying: The apply program is writing the files and reloading nginx.
guide.cstate.approved: Approved; waiting for its turn at the apply program.
guide.cstate.failed: A check did not pass. Run the checks again or propose a corrected change.
guide.cstate.pending_approval: Every check passed; waiting for an approver.
guide.cstate.rejected: An approver rejected it, with a note.
guide.cstate.rolled_back: Was in production; an earlier version was restored later.
guide.detail.internal: Stopped by an internal error; the previous files were restored.
guide.detail.overridden: Did not pass; overridden with a justification
guide.detail.rolled_back: Replaced later by restoring an earlier version
guide.detail.title: Where this change stands
guide.ev.audit_d: ModSecurity writes the request and every rule it matched to its JSON audit log.
guide.ev.collect_d: The collector picks up new lines every few seconds, masks passwords and tokens, marks the source internal or external with the internal address list from the settings, and stores the result.
guide.ev.decide_d: An external source is blocked with 403 when it hits a confident-block rule, or when its score reaches the CRS inbound threshold (if blocking over the threshold is switched on). Internal addresses and everything else are only logged.
guide.ev.list_d: One row per request. Open a row to see the rules it matched, then decide whether a change is needed.
guide.ev.note: "Blocked" means the engine was on for that request and the answer was 403 (or 400 for a malformed request body). "Decided by" tells which rule made the call: a confident rule, the CRS score, the fallback rule or another rule.
guide.ev.request_d: A browser, app or scanner sends a request to one of the sites behind nginx.
guide.ev.rules_d: Every CRS rule that matches adds points to the request's anomaly score. The site's own rules (exclusions, confident blocks) run in the same pass.
guide.ev.title: How a request becomes an event here
guide.evd.decide_d: Legitimate request blocked: create an exclusion. Attack that got through: create a similar block. Expected result: nothing to do.
guide.evd.title: Where this event stands
guide.first.check_d: System check shows the service, integrity, time sync and backups at a glance (admin).
guide.first.events_d: Filter by site, outcome, rule or source; open one to see the request and every rule it hit.
guide.first.lookup_d: Everything one source did, to tell a false positive from an attack.
guide.first.overview_d: Blocked and logged traffic over time; the top sites, attack types, sources and rules.
guide.first.propose_d: Exclude a false positive or block an attack (operator and above); it then goes through checks, the sandbox and approval.
guide.first.signin_d: Change the temporary password; approvers and admins set up TOTP.
guide.first.title: First sign-in
guide.intro: What each part does, the first things to look at, how a rule change travels from proposal to production, and what each role may do.
guide.ip.attack: Real attack? Propose a confident block
guide.ip.attack_d: From an event, "Create similar block" drafts a rule for the same path. It only blocks external sources.
guide.ip.events_d: Look at the paths, the status codes and whether the requests were blocked.
guide.ip.fp_d: Open one of its events and use "Create exclusion for this": the draft is limited to that site and path, and to the rules and fields it matched.
guide.ip.look_d: See how many events it caused in 7 and 30 days, on which sites, and which rules it hit.
guide.ip.note: Nothing changes on the site until a change passes the checks and the sandbox test and is approved by a person. Confident-block rules never block internal addresses.
guide.ip.rules_d: Open a rule to read what it looks for and how often it fires for everyone else.
guide.ip.title: How to investigate a source address
guide.node.analyst.desc: Groups recent events into candidates on a schedule and asks the configured LLM server in batches; the program validates the answer, proposes narrow blocks or exclusions as ordinary changes and opens alerts for what needs following up. It never approves or writes rules; loosening always waits for a person.
guide.node.analyst.name: Event analysis
guide.node.apply.desc: The only part that runs as root, started by systemd when an approved change is queued. It validates the request again, saves the current files, checks the health-check URLs, writes the new files, runs nginx -t, reloads, confirms the reload took effect and checks the URLs again. Any failure restores the previous files. It refuses to run when its own files do not match the signed release.
guide.node.apply.name: Apply program
guide.node.auditlog.desc: ModSecurity writes one JSON record for each request that matched rules: the request, every rule it hit, the score and whether it was blocked.
guide.node.auditlog.name: Audit log
guide.node.channels.desc: E-mail, Telegram, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Discord, Zulip, Nextcloud Talk and a generic webhook (HMAC signature). Values from requests never become markup, links or mentions.
guide.node.channels.name: Channels
guide.node.clients.desc: Browsers, apps and bots on the internet and on the internal network. Every request reaches nginx first.
guide.node.clients.name: Visitors
guide.node.collector.desc: Follows the audit log, turns every record into an event and stores it with hourly statistics.
guide.node.collector.name: Collector
guide.node.database.desc: SQLite: events, statistics, changes, versions, accounts and the hash-chained audit trail. File mode 0600, owned by the service user; sensitive request values are masked before they are stored.
guide.node.database.name: Database
guide.node.llm.desc: An OpenAI-compatible LLM server (llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama…) set in Settings. The request data sent to it is always marked untrusted; the answer is constrained by a JSON schema.
guide.node.llm.name: LLM server
guide.node.managed.desc: The site's own rules (exclusions, blocks, redactions) that nginx loads together with the CRS. After adoption only the apply program writes them; an edit made any other way is detected, and changes stop until it is resolved.
guide.node.managed.name: Site rule files
guide.node.monitor.desc: Verifies the audit hash chain and writes anchors (every 5 minutes, full check daily), checks the installed program against the signed manifest (hourly), fingerprints the nginx / ModSecurity / CRS files (every 5 minutes), expires dormant accounts and makes the daily backup. Problems become integrity.* audit rows at syslog priority crit.
guide.node.monitor.name: Integrity monitor
guide.node.nginx.desc: The reverse proxy. On every request ModSecurity runs the OWASP Core Rule Set and the site's own rules. Each matching CRS rule adds to an anomaly score; a request whose score reaches the blocking threshold gets 403, a lower score passes and the matches are only logged. Site rules can also block or exclude directly.
guide.node.nginx.name: nginx + WAF
guide.node.notify.desc: The web service and the other units only queue notifications in the database; this unit sends them to each channel, retries failures, limits each channel per hour and reminds open alerts. The web service itself never connects out.
guide.node.notify.name: Notifications
guide.node.sandbox.desc: Before approval, a change is tested in a temporary nginx on 127.0.0.1 with the candidate rules: the test requests and the saved regression samples must give the expected results. Production is not touched.
guide.node.sandbox.name: Sandbox
guide.node.siem.desc: Every audit row and every anchor also goes to syslog, so a separate system keeps a copy this host cannot change. Alert on integrity.* events.
guide.node.siem.name: Syslog / SIEM
guide.node.sites.desc: The services behind the reverse proxy. Only requests the WAF lets through reach them.
guide.node.sites.name: Websites
guide.node.users.desc: People sign in with a password (plus TOTP for approvers and admins). Other systems use API tokens limited by scope, source network and expiry; a token can propose a change but never approve one.
guide.node.users.name: People + tokens
guide.node.webui.desc: This interface and the REST API, reached only through the internal management site. Every action is written to the audit trail.
guide.node.webui.name: Web UI + API
guide.node.workflow.desc: Proposals from people or API tokens get static checks, evidence from past traffic and a sandbox run, then wait for approval. Only approved changes are handed to the apply program.
guide.node.workflow.name: Change workflow
guide.release.apply_d: The root apply program runs the same check before it handles any request.
guide.release.check_d: The service compares the installed files with the signed list every hour (default; [integrity] program_check_minutes) and on "Run checks now". A failure writes integrity.program_failed at syslog priority crit.
guide.release.install_d: install.sh checks the signature and every file before installing. The first install pins the key ({key}); a release signed with another key is refused unless --accept-new-key is given.
guide.release.note: A copy run from a source tree is not checked (status: not installed).
guide.release.refuse_d: If a file was changed, added or removed, the apply program refuses to run, so no nginx change is made with modified code.
guide.release.sign_d: Each release lists the SHA-256 of every file it ships (MANIFEST.sha256), signed with the project's release key (RSA-3072).
guide.release.title: How the program is protected
guide.roles.admin: Also manages accounts, API tokens and settings, adopts rule files, and sees the audit trail, system check, compliance and backups. Needs TOTP.
guide.roles.approver: Also approves or rejects changes, rolls back versions and reviews configuration changes made outside. Needs TOTP.
guide.roles.note: Each role includes everything of the roles before it.
guide.roles.operator: Also proposes and prepares changes: preview, re-run checks, cancel, manage regression samples.
guide.roles.title: Roles
guide.roles.viewer: Sees events, rules, sites, changes and versions (read only).
guide.rule.hit_d: CRS rules add points to the anomaly score; site rules can skip checks (exclusions) or block outright (confident blocks).
guide.rule.note: Start from one event when you can: its page has "Create exclusion for this" and "Create similar block", which fill in the draft for you.
guide.rule.process_d: The change is checked against past events, tested in a sandbox and approved by a person before it is applied.
guide.rule.propose_d: False positive: an exclusion for that site and path. An attack that got through: a confident block.
guide.rule.record_d: Every event keeps the rules it matched, and hits are counted per day for this list.
guide.rule.review_d: Who sent them, to which site and path, and were they blocked? Many hits from your own users on one path usually mean a false positive.
guide.rule.title: What a rule hit means and what to do next
guide.title: How it works
guide.token.call_d: It sends the header Authorization: Bearer jwm_…
guide.token.create_d: An administrator picks the scopes and, optionally, source networks and an end date. The token is shown once; only its SHA-256 is stored.
guide.token.done_d: Every allowed request is recorded in the audit log (token.used) and updates "Last used".
guide.token.note: A token can never approve or reject changes, manage users or tokens, change or read settings, read the audit log or use the account pages: those need a person who is signed in. With changes:propose it can only propose; a person approves.
guide.token.scope_d: Each endpoint needs one scope. Without it the request is refused and recorded (token.denied).
guide.token.source_d: If source networks are set, a request from any other address is refused and recorded (token.denied).
guide.token.title: What happens to a request with a token
guide.token.valid_d: Unknown, revoked or expired tokens are refused.
guide.user.active_d: Normal work. Every sign-in and action is recorded in the audit log.
guide.user.active_d_age: Normal work. After {n} days the password must be changed at the next sign-in.
guide.user.create_d: An administrator adds the account with a role and, for a temporary account, an end date.
guide.user.disabled_d: By an administrator, or automatically (checked every hour) when the end date has passed or there was no sign-in until the "Dormant on" date. All its sessions end. The last active administrator is never disabled automatically.
guide.user.first_pw: The user must replace it with an own password (at least {n} characters).
guide.user.first_pw_any: The user must replace it with an own password.
guide.user.first_totp: {roles} must also set up two-factor authentication (TOTP) before they can continue.
guide.user.first_totp_none: Two-factor authentication is optional for every role.
guide.user.first_totp_some: Roles that require two-factor authentication (TOTP) must set it up before they can continue.
guide.user.locked_d: Too many wrong passwords in a row lock the account for a while. It unlocks by itself, or an administrator unlocks it here.
guide.user.note: Reset password gives a new temporary password and removes two-factor authentication: the user starts again at the first sign-in. Enable brings a disabled account back.
guide.user.temp_d: A random temporary password is shown here once. Hand it over through a safe channel.
guide.user.title: Account lifecycle
guide.versions.after_d: Changes applied after the restored version are marked “rolled back”; their rule IDs stay reserved.
guide.versions.apply_d: The restore goes straight to the apply program: snapshot, nginx -t, reload, health checks, automatic restore on failure. There is no sandbox run and no second approval.
guide.versions.current_d: The version in production is “applied (current)”; the previous one becomes “superseded”. A failed apply leaves the previous version current, and the next apply reuses the failed number.
guide.versions.new_d: Each apply (change, adoption or restore) gets the next version number and keeps the complete files with their checksums.
guide.versions.note: Possible only while nothing else is being applied; the current version cannot be restored onto itself.
guide.versions.restore_d: An approver picks an earlier applied or superseded version and writes a note. It is written again as a new version; the history is kept.
guide.versions.title: How versions and restoring work
guide.wf.applied_d: State: applied. A new version of the managed files is in production and can be restored later from Versions.
guide.wf.apply_d: State: applying. The only part that runs as root writes the files and reloads nginx (steps below).
guide.wf.approval_d: State: pending approval. An approver or administrator who did not propose it approves or rejects (adoption: administrators only). Loosening always needs a person; API tokens can never approve.
guide.wf.evidence_d: From the access logs and the event history. A block must not match any external request that succeeded (2xx/3xx) or any internal source except known scanners. An exclusion shows which past alerts disappear and flags external ones that look like attacks.
guide.wf.note: A failed check puts the change in “checks failed”: run the checks again or propose a corrected change; a failed evidence check can be overridden with a written justification (recorded, still needs approval, never applied automatically). Single-admin mode (Settings) lets the proposer approve their own change; approving one's own loosening then needs a fresh TOTP code and a note of at least 10 characters. If enabled, a new confident block with clean evidence and passing checks is applied without approval, up to a daily limit.
guide.wf.propose_d: An operator (or an API token allowed to propose) picks a template, fills it in and writes a reason. State: checking.
guide.wf.queue_d: State: approved. One apply at a time. If another version was applied after the checks, the checks run again first.
guide.wf.sandbox_d: A throwaway nginx with the production configuration plus this change replays your test cases and their encoding and case variants. For tightening, every regression sample is replayed too: none may get a 403.
guide.wf.states: States a change can be in
guide.wf.static_d: The rule is generated and the whole managed file must pass the expert-mode checks: allowed directives only, no duplicate rule IDs.
guide.wf.title: From proposal to production
guide.wizard.after_d: When every check passes it waits for an approver; then the apply program puts it in production.
guide.wizard.scope_d: Site, path, rule and field, as narrow as possible. The preview checks the form as you type and shows the generated rule.
guide.wizard.submit_d: The change is saved as “checking”; the static check, evidence and sandbox run in the background.
guide.wizard.template_d: Pick what you want to achieve; the template writes the rule for you.
guide.wizard.tests_d: Add requests the sandbox must block or allow, and explain why the change is needed.
guide.wizard.title: Creating a change
guide.wizard.tpl.confident_block: Blocks an unmistakable attack pattern in the path, URL, User-Agent, Host or a header, for external sources only.
guide.wizard.tpl.country: Limit one site by country (only these, or not these), with daily lists from the five regional registries. Never refuses internal networks, scanners or the CDN.
guide.wizard.tpl.exclusion: Fixes a false positive: one rule stops looking at one field (or one request) on one site or path, and everything else stays protected.
guide.wizard.tpl.plugin: Turns on a CRS plugin (for example the WordPress or Nextcloud exclusions) for one site.
guide.wizard.tpl.raw: Administrators only: a SecRule you write yourself, checked against a list of forbidden directives; when its effect is unclear it counts as loosening.
guide.wizard.tpl.redaction: Tells CRS not to inspect fields such as passwords, so their values never reach the audit log.
ipcard.open: Click the address for everything about it.
login.subtitle: Sign in to manage the web application firewall.

waf.intro: Drawn from the configuration that is in effect now (nginx + ModSecurity files): which mechanisms exist, which of them block, which only log or add score, and which loosen the checks — for requests from outside and from the internal networks.
waf.note.eval_mixed: blocks only when an earlier rule turned blocking on for the request ({ids}); otherwise only logs.
waf.note.logs: the engine is {mode} for this source here, so a deny is only logged.
waf.note.not_applicable: the rules' source condition excludes this source.
waf.note.not_reached: the rules only act on a mark that no rule sets for this source.
waf.note.switched: blocking is turned on for single requests by rule(s) {ids}.
waf.redirect_hint: This block only sends clients elsewhere (http to https): nothing in it for the WAF to protect.
waf.score.hint: Each CRS match adds points by severity. A request is judged against the threshold {n}; the bars show how many matches of one severity reach it.
waf.score.legend_below: one match, still under the threshold
waf.score.legend_reach: the match that reaches the threshold

waf.stage.confident.desc: Site rules for requests that are certainly attacks (a path, a file name, a header…), usually limited to some sources. When one matches it marks the request and turns blocking on for that request only, so the CRS decision or the fallback rule refuses it.
waf.stage.crs_detect.desc: The CRS rules of the active paranoia level look for attack patterns. Every match adds points by its severity; nothing is blocked in this step.
waf.stage.crs_eval.desc: CRS compares the total inbound anomaly score with the threshold ({n}). At or over it the rule denies — but a deny only blocks when the engine is On for that request; with {mode} it is only logged.
waf.stage.deny_rules.desc: Other rules with deny (for example ModSecurity's own request body checks). They block only when the engine is On for the request; otherwise they only log.
waf.stage.engine.desc: SecRuleEngine decides whether a deny really blocks: DetectionOnly only logs, On blocks. A rule can switch it on for one request (ctl:ruleEngine=On) and a vhost can set its own mode.
waf.stage.exclusions.desc: Rules that make the WAF less strict for some requests: they remove CRS rules or inspected fields (ctl:ruleRemove…, SecRuleRemoveById, SecRuleUpdateTargetById), switch body inspection off, allow, enable exclusion plugins or widen the allowed methods and types. They run first (or when the configuration is loaded), so the later steps never see what they removed.
waf.stage.fallback.desc: A deny for requests an earlier rule marked (for example a confident match whose score stayed under the threshold).
waf.stage.not_inspected.desc: Requests to vhosts without the WAF, to locations with "modsecurity off", or after a rule turned the engine Off never reach the checks below: nothing is scored, logged or blocked.
waf.stage.other.desc: Site rules this diagram cannot classify. Check their id and message in the table.
waf.stage.outcome.desc: What happens to a request from each source in the end.
waf.stage.settings.desc: Rules that change settings for some requests (thresholds, paranoia level, body processor). They do not block by themselves.
waf.stage.site_scoring.desc: Site rules that add anomaly points (for example the points of a confident match), so that the CRS threshold check decides.
waf.stage.threshold_block.desc: Site rules after CRS that read the CRS score themselves: when it reached the threshold (and the source matches their condition) they turn blocking on and refuse the request, even though the global engine only logs.

wfs.auto_tighten_analyst: Apply the event analysis' confident blocks automatically too
wfs.auto_tighten_analyst_hint: Same conditions as above (external sources only, clean evidence, sandbox passed, daily limit); a notification follows. Loosening (exclusions for false positives) and blocks that include internal sources always wait for a person.
wfs.auto_tighten_hint: Only new confident blocks on the URL, file name or headers (never the body), external sources only, with clean evidence (no external 2xx/3xx, no internal hits) and every sandbox test passed. Anything else waits for approval.
wfs.health_from_nginx: Sites nginx serves (click to add or remove; https when the site listens with ssl):
wfs.health_urls_hint: One per line. Requested through this host's nginx (127.0.0.1, with the site name) before and after every apply; any status difference restores the previous files.
wfs.sandbox_available: The sandbox can run on this host.
wfs.sandbox_required_off: Without the sandbox, changes are only checked statically before they reach production.
wfs.sandbox_unavailable: The sandbox cannot run on this host (nginx binary or ModSecurity configuration not found).
wfs.single_admin_mode_hint: Lets the proposer approve their own change. Approving one's own loosening still needs a fresh TOTP code and a note. Every use is recorded. Leave off when there are two or more approvers.

wizard.action_hint.body_processor: For clients that send a body in another format than their Content-Type says.
wizard.action_hint.remove_rule: The listed rules do not run at all for these requests. Prefer ignoring a field if you can.
wizard.action_hint.remove_tag: A whole class of rules is switched off for these requests.
wizard.action_hint.remove_target_by_id: The listed rules stop looking at the listed fields here; everything else is still inspected.
wizard.action_hint.remove_target_by_tag: Every rule with the tag stops looking at the listed fields here (e.g. OWASP_CRS for free text).
wizard.action_hint.score_only: CRS still scores and logs, confident blocks still apply; only "over the threshold → block" is dropped here.
wizard.action_opt.body_processor: Parse the body as another format
wizard.action_opt.remove_tag: A whole rule class not run
wizard.action_opt.remove_target_by_tag: Rules with a tag ignore field(s)
wizard.action_opt.score_only: Score only, never block on the score
wizard.before_rule_id_hint: Rule ID of a managed rule in the same file. Empty: at the end of the file. Order matters when a later rule reads what this one sets (e.g. before 10299, which refuses requests marked for blocking).
wizard.block_intro: Blocks external requests matching a clear attack shape. Internal sources are never blocked; CRS's 949110 takes the decision.
wizard.block_source_all_note: Internal sources are blocked too. The evidence check fails if any internal address other than a known scanner made such a request, and this change is never applied automatically. The known scanner list is written into the rule as it is now; after changing the list, propose the rule again.
wizard.confirm_tag: I understand that a whole rule class is switched off here
wizard.country_intro: Limit one site by where requests come from: only the countries you list, or every country except them. The address lists come from the five regional Internet registries and are refreshed daily.
wizard.country_limits: Registry data says where an address block was registered, not where its user is (a VPN, a cloud region or a roaming phone can be elsewhere). It works through ModSecurity: locations with modsecurity off are not covered. Behind a CDN the site needs set_real_ip_from / real_ip_header.
wizard.country_never: Never refused: the internal networks, the known scanners, the trusted proxies and the protected list (Settings > Temporary IP blocks), so a CDN in front of the site is not shut out.
wizard.country_no_data: The country lists have not been downloaded yet. Use "Update now" in Settings, then try again.
wizard.exceptions: Exceptions (paths, one regular expression per line)
wizard.exceptions_hint: For example WebDAV or share links, where sync clients legitimately fetch .env or .git files.
wizard.exclusion_intro: Narrowest first: one site, one path, one rule, one field. The rule keeps protecting everything else.
wizard.external_only: Applies to external sources only; internal sources are only logged.
wizard.kind: What do you want to do?
wizard.kind_hint.confident_block: An attack shape: block it for external sources, with evidence that no one legitimate is hit.
wizard.kind_hint.country: Where requests come from: one site only for some countries, or not for some countries.
wizard.kind_hint.exclusion: A false positive: stop one rule from looking at one thing, as narrowly as possible.
wizard.kind_hint.plugin: Turn on a CRS plugin (WordPress, Nextcloud…) for one site.
wizard.kind_hint.raw: Write a SecRule yourself (administrators only, checked against a forbidden list).
wizard.kind_hint.redaction: Passwords and secrets: never inspected, so never copied into the audit log.
wizard.loosen_note: This change loosens the WAF: a person has to approve it, whatever the checks say.
wizard.lowercase_note: Matched after lowercasing (and, for paths, URL-decoding and normalizing): write the expression in lowercase.
wizard.plugin_intro: CRS plugins are off by default and turned on per site.
wizard.preview_empty: Fill in the form to see the generated rule.
wizard.raw_warning: Expert mode: the text is used as written. Engine-wide settings, audit settings, Include, exec, file operators and removing system rules are refused.
wizard.reason_ph: What happened, which evidence, why this is the narrowest change
wizard.redaction_intro: These fields are never inspected by CRS, so their values never end up in the audit log.
wizard.remove_tag_warning: Warning: this switches off an entire class of rules (for example every SQL injection rule) for these requests. Use it only if field-level exclusions cannot work.
wizard.score_only_explain: Use for endpoints whose body is what people type: saving drafts, sending mail or chat messages. Code, paths and commands there are normal and should not get a user blocked by the anomaly score.
wizard.submit_hint: Static check, evidence and sandbox run next; then it waits for approval.
wizard.tests_hint.block: At least one external request that must be blocked (403). Encoding, case and slash variants and the same request from an internal source are added automatically, plus each site's regression samples.
wizard.tests_hint.country: Tests are added for you: a request from a country that passes, one from a country that is refused, and one from inside.
wizard.tests_hint.other: Replay the request that caused the false positive; list the excluded rules under "Rules that must not match".
